title: Baruch atah
hook: read the opening words of every blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shema Yisrael: a silent eye, and a dot that moved to the left. Your line: read it yourself. Today, two more words, the ones that open a blessing.

Friday evening, a kitchen. Two candles are lit, and before anyone eats, someone lifts a cup of wine and starts to speak. Then a hand rests on the bread, and someone speaks again. A new fruit in season, a glass of water, thunder outside, new clothes put on for the first time: the prayer book has a blessing for each, and the formula opens the same way. Two words first, over and over, like the first two notes of a song the whole family knows. Baruch atah. Learn to read them, and you'll see them at the top of page after page.
screen: `CANDLES, WINE, BREAD.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH.` → `THE SAME TWO WORDS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Baruch atah. Turn it four ways. First, baruch. Bet, with a dot inside so it says b, not v, and the T-shaped mark under it: ba. Resh, then a vav with a dot in its belly, which says oo: ru. At the end, the long-tailed final chaf, one of the five endings, a breathy ch. Ba, ruch. Baruch. Blessed. Second, atah. Alef, silent, carrying a short line: ah. Tav, with a dot inside and the T-shaped mark: ta. Then heh, silent at the end of the word. A, tah. Atah. You. Third, who "you" is. The words are already in Psalm 119: "Blessed art Thou, O LORD; teach me Thy statutes." After baruch atah comes the name of God, which isn't read as written: in prayer it's said Adonai, and outside prayer some say Hashem, the Name. Then come the words for our God, king of the world. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, records two teachers' views: a blessing without the Name is not a blessing, and a blessing without God's kingship is not a blessing. Fourth, a turn some readers notice. Baruch atah speaks straight to God: you. But the blessing over bread goes on, hamotzi, who brings forth bread from the earth, and moves from speaking to God to speaking about God. Close and far in a single sentence. The blessing begins face to face.
screen: `BARUCH: BA, RUCH, BLESSED.` · `ATAH: A, TAH, YOU.` · `THEN THE NAME, AND THE KING.` · `FACE TO FACE, THEN ABOUT.` · then, large: `בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה`

segments.voice: Read the screen from the right, ba, ruch, baruch, then a, tah, atah, aloud once slowly so you hear each letter, then again more smoothly. Let them go and sit with the shape they leave, someone speaking directly, saying you, and notice one thing in front of you: a cup, a window, your own hands. If you pray, you can say a blessing you know over it.
Baruch atah. Blessed are you: the two words that open the blessings, read in Hebrew, right to left. Today's word.
Your line: baruch atah. Two words, and the blessing is already face to face. Go gently.

howItsDone: Jews say blessings before eating and drinking, over Sabbath candles and wine, and at many other moments; the standard blessing opens with baruch atah, then God's name, read Adonai, and the words for king of the world.
